title: Cache eviction in TanStack Query and SWR: staleTime, gcTime & LRU
description: You probably use TanStack Query or SWR every day. Start with a familiar puzzle, 'why did React Query refetch this?', and learn how `staleTime` and `gcTime` decide when cached data is refetched or dropped. Then trace an LRU cache built from a hash map and a doubly linked list, compare it with LFU and TTL, and see why a memo `Map` with no size limit leaks memory.

questions.title: Why did React Query refetch this?
questions.description: A component calls `useQuery({ queryKey: ['user', 7], queryFn })` with TanStack Query's **default** options. On mount, the cached user appears instantly. Then a network request fires and the data refreshes. The query key never changed.

images.alt: One TanStack Query entry with two independent clocks. The staleTime bar shows a zero-width FRESH band followed by a wide STALE band where the cached value still renders instantly and a background refetch is allowed. The gcTime bar shows ACTIVE, with at least one mounted observer and never garbage-collected, next to a dashed INACTIVE box where the entry is removed five minutes after the last observer unmounts. A card lists the three default refetch triggers (refetchOnMount, refetchOnWindowFocus, refetchOnReconnect) and notes that just reading the cached value isn't one of them.
images.caption: A zero-width FRESH band means the cached data was already stale on mount.

options.text: The default `staleTime` is `0`, so the cached data was already stale, and mounting triggered a background refetch (`refetchOnMount`).
A built-in LRU size cap evicted the entry, so the data had to be fetched from scratch.
The `gcTime` timer elapsed and garbage-collected the cache entry, forcing a reload.
Reading the query created a brand-new cache entry under a different key.

questions.explanation:
TanStack Query follows *stale-while-revalidate*: it shows cached data **right away**, then decides whether to refresh it in the background. Two defaults cause the refetch here:

- `staleTime: 0`: data goes stale as soon as it arrives, so it's always eligible for a refetch.
- `refetchOnMount: true`: when a new observer mounts on a stale query, a background refetch starts. `refetchOnWindowFocus` and `refetchOnReconnect` work the same way.

Nothing was evicted. You *saw* the cached data, so the entry was still there. A component was mounted, so the query was active and the `gcTime` timer wasn't running. An LRU cap and `gcTime` both describe **removing** entries, and neither happened here. To stop the refetch, raise `staleTime` (for example, `staleTime: 60_000`). SWR behaves the same way: `useSWR` returns cached data and revalidates on focus and reconnect by default.

questions.title: What's the difference between `staleTime` and `gcTime`?
questions.description: In TanStack Query v5, `gcTime` is the new name for `cacheTime`.

images.alt: One TanStack Query entry with two independent clocks. The staleTime bar shows a zero-width FRESH band followed by a wide STALE band where the cached value still renders instantly and a background refetch is allowed. The gcTime bar shows ACTIVE, with at least one mounted observer and never garbage-collected, next to a dashed INACTIVE box where the entry is removed five minutes after the last observer unmounts. A card lists the three default refetch triggers (refetchOnMount, refetchOnWindowFocus, refetchOnReconnect) and notes that just reading the cached value isn't one of them.
images.caption: Two bars, two clocks: freshness on top, retention below.

options.text: `staleTime` is how long data stays *fresh* (no background refetch). `gcTime` is how long an **inactive** query, one with no mounted observers, stays in the cache before it's removed.
They're the same option: `gcTime` is just the v5 name for `staleTime`.
`staleTime` deletes the entry from the cache, while `gcTime` keeps a stale copy around.
`gcTime` must be smaller than `staleTime`, or the cache throws an error.

questions.explanation:
The two timers answer different questions:

- **`staleTime`** (default `0`): how long is this data fresh? While it's fresh, mounting, window focus, and reconnecting don't trigger a background refetch. It never removes anything.
- **`gcTime`** (default `5 * 60 * 1000`, or 5 minutes): once nothing uses this query, how long until its memory is freed? The timer starts only when the query goes **inactive**, meaning its last observer unmounts. If the query becomes active again before the timer runs out, the cached data is reused.

`gcTime` is the v5 name for `cacheTime`, **not** for `staleTime`. Nothing requires `gcTime < staleTime`. You usually want `gcTime` to be longer, so a remounted query still finds its data (even if it's stale) and revalidates instead of starting from nothing.

questions.title: Which key does the LRU cache evict when `put('D', 4)` runs?

images.alt: An LRU cache of capacity 3. A row of hash-map cells for "A", "B" and "C" points down at three doubly linked nodes A, B and C joined by two-headed prev/next arrows, with the LRU end on the left and the MRU end on the right. A note says O(1) splicing needs both links. Below, three steps: after put A, put B and put C the order is A, B, C; get('A') moves A to the MRU end leaving B, C, A; put('D',4) exceeds capacity, so the LRU end B is evicted and the order becomes C, A, D.
images.caption: Step three: the LRU end after `get('A')` is `B`.

questions.explanation:
Here's the recency order, from least to most recently used:

```text
put('A',1) -> [A]
put('B',2) -> [A, B]
put('C',3) -> [A, B, C]
get('A')   -> [B, C, A]   // A touched -> moved to the MRU end
put('D',4) -> over capacity -> evict LRU 'B' -> [C, A, D]
```

It's tempting to pick `A` because it was inserted first, but LRU evicts by **last use**, not insertion order. `get('A')` moved `A` to the most-recently-used end. That left `B`, untouched since it was inserted, as the least recently used key. After the insert the order is `[C, A, D]`, so `C` is next to go.

questions.title: Why does an LRU cache's list need to be **doubly** linked?
questions.description: The textbook O(1) LRU cache pairs a hash map (key → node) with a linked list that orders nodes by recency.

images.alt: An LRU cache of capacity 3. A row of hash-map cells for "A", "B" and "C" points down at three doubly linked nodes A, B and C joined by two-headed prev/next arrows, with the LRU end on the left and the MRU end on the right. A note says O(1) splicing needs both links. Below, three steps: after put A, put B and put C the order is A, B, C; get('A') moves A to the MRU end leaving B, C, A; put('D',4) exceeds capacity, so the LRU end B is evicted and the order becomes C, A, D.
images.caption: The two-headed arrows matter: without both links, there's no O(1) splice.

options.text: Moving or removing any node in O(1) means rewiring both of its neighbors, and a singly linked list can only find a node's predecessor with an O(n) scan.
A doubly linked list lets you binary-search the keys in O(log n).
Two pointers per node are needed so each entry can store both its key and its value.
Singly linked lists can't be traversed in order, so iteration would be impossible.

questions.explanation:
Every `get` or `put` hit **moves a node to the most-recently-used end**, and every eviction **unlinks the least-recently-used node**. Both remove a node from wherever it sits in the list. To do that in O(1), you rewire its previous and next neighbors:

```text
prev <-> node <-> next   becomes   prev <-> next
```

A *singly* linked list only has `next` pointers, so finding a node's predecessor means walking from the head. That's O(n), which defeats the point of an O(1) cache. The hash map handles O(1) key→node lookup, and the doubly linked list handles O(1) reordering. Nothing searches by walking the list (that's the map's job), so the binary-search and traversal options are distractors.

questions.title: What happens to this memo `Map` on a long-running server?

options.text: The `Map` grows forever, keeping every id, its value, and anything that value references alive for the life of the process. It's a memory leak.
Nothing leaks: once a `reqId` goes out of scope elsewhere, the garbage collector removes its `Map` entry automatically.
V8 caps a `Map` at 1024 entries, so memory levels off.
Because keys are unique, each call overwrites the previous entry, so memory stays about the same.

questions.explanation:
A `Map` holds **strong references** to its keys and values, so an entry stays until you `delete` it or drop the whole `Map`. With a new unique id on every request, the cache only grows. The garbage collector can't help: the `Map` is reachable, so everything in it is reachable too.

Two fixes:

- Cap the cache with an eviction policy (LRU, LFU, or TTL) so old entries get removed.
- If your keys are objects and an entry should live only as long as its key, use a `WeakMap`. Its entries can be garbage-collected once nothing else references the key. A `WeakMap` can't take primitive keys like a numeric id and isn't iterable, so it won't help when you need a size cap.

questions.title: Which statements about a hash map + doubly linked list LRU cache are true?

images.alt: An LRU cache of capacity 3. A row of hash-map cells for "A", "B" and "C" points down at three doubly linked nodes A, B and C joined by two-headed prev/next arrows, with the LRU end on the left and the MRU end on the right. A note says O(1) splicing needs both links. Below, three steps: after put A, put B and put C the order is A, B, C; get('A') moves A to the MRU end leaving B, C, A; put('D',4) exceeds capacity, so the LRU end B is evicted and the order becomes C, A, D.
images.caption: Map cells for lookup, list order for recency, LRU end for eviction.

options.text: On a cache **hit**, `get` moves the accessed node to the most-recently-used end so it isn't evicted next.
The hash map stores each key's node, so lookup is O(1) without scanning the list.
When `put` exceeds capacity, the node at the least-recently-used end is unlinked **and** its key is deleted from the map.
Nodes are kept in sorted key order so the cache can answer range queries.

questions.explanation:
The two structures split the work. The **map** answers *where is this key's node?* in O(1). The **doubly linked list** keeps the recency order and supports O(1) splicing.

- On a hit, move the node to the MRU end, or the recency order goes stale.
- Look keys up through the map in O(1). You never walk the list to find one.
- On overflow, drop the node at the LRU end **and** delete its key from the map. Forgetting the map deletion is the classic bug: it leaks memory, and the map's `size` drifts out of sync with the list.

The list is ordered by **recency**, not by key, so it can't answer range or sorted queries. For that you'd need something like a balanced BST.

questions.title: Which statements about LRU, LFU, and TTL eviction are true?

options.text: LRU evicts the entry that has gone the longest without being accessed.
LFU evicts the entry with the fewest accesses. Raw counts don't decay, so an entry that was briefly popular can stick around long after it stops being useful.
TTL evicts an entry once its age exceeds a fixed lifetime, regardless of how recently or often it was used.
A pure TTL policy guarantees the cache never holds more than a fixed number of entries.

questions.explanation:
Each policy looks at a different signal:

- **LRU** (recency) evicts the entry used least recently. It works well when recently used items are likely to be used again.
- **LFU** (frequency) evicts the entry used least often. Its classic weakness is **cache pollution**: an item that was once very popular keeps its high count and never gets evicted, unless you add aging or decay (for example, counting only within a time window).
- **TTL** (age) evicts on a timer, no matter how recently or often the entry was used. It fits data that goes out of date after a known time.

The false statement mixes up *age* and *count*. TTL limits how **old** an entry can be, not how **many** entries exist. If 10,000 different keys arrive within one TTL window, all 10,000 sit in the cache at once. To limit size, you need a count-based policy like LRU or LFU, often combined with TTL.

questions.title: What makes TanStack Query refetch a stale query?
questions.description: Assume **default** options and a query that is currently stale.

images.alt: One TanStack Query entry with two independent clocks. The staleTime bar shows a zero-width FRESH band followed by a wide STALE band where the cached value still renders instantly and a background refetch is allowed. The gcTime bar shows ACTIVE, with at least one mounted observer and never garbage-collected, next to a dashed INACTIVE box where the entry is removed five minutes after the last observer unmounts. A card lists the three default refetch triggers (refetchOnMount, refetchOnWindowFocus, refetchOnReconnect) and notes that just reading the cached value isn't one of them.
images.caption: The three chips are the default triggers. Reading the cache isn't one of them.

options.text: A component mounts and becomes a new observer of the query (`refetchOnMount`).
The browser tab or window regains focus (`refetchOnWindowFocus`).
The network reconnects after the device was offline (`refetchOnReconnect`).
Another component reads the already-cached value, with no mount, focus, or reconnect event.

questions.explanation:
TanStack Query's automatic refetch options are all `true` by default, and each one fires only when the query is **stale**. With `staleTime: 0`, that's right away.

- `refetchOnMount`: a new observer mounts.
- `refetchOnWindowFocus`: the user comes back to the tab.
- `refetchOnReconnect`: the network comes back.

Just reading cached data doesn't trigger a fetch. Selecting an existing entry returns it synchronously. Without a mount, focus, or reconnect event (or an explicit `refetch()`, `invalidateQueries`, or `refetchInterval`), no request goes out. SWR has the same options under different names: `revalidateOnFocus` and `revalidateOnReconnect`.

questions.title: Which statements about a plain JS `Map` are true?
questions.description: You want an LRU-style cache capped at 100 entries, built on a plain JS `Map`. Select **all** that apply.

options.text: `cache.keys().next().value` returns the **oldest inserted** key, because `Map` iterates in insertion order. That makes it a handy eviction target.
Calling `cache.set(key, v)` on an existing key updates the value but does **not** move the key to the end of the iteration order.
To approximate LRU, on each hit you `delete` the key and `set` it again, which moves it to the most-recently-used end.
`cache.set` automatically discards the oldest entry once `size` reaches 100, so no manual eviction is needed.

questions.title: After how many minutes is an inactive query garbage-collected?
questions.description: Assume TanStack Query v5 with default settings. An **inactive** query has no mounted observers. Enter the number of minutes.

images.alt: One TanStack Query entry with two independent clocks. The staleTime bar shows a zero-width FRESH band followed by a wide STALE band where the cached value still renders instantly and a background refetch is allowed. The gcTime bar shows ACTIVE, with at least one mounted observer and never garbage-collected, next to a dashed INACTIVE box where the entry is removed five minutes after the last observer unmounts. A card lists the three default refetch triggers (refetchOnMount, refetchOnWindowFocus, refetchOnReconnect) and notes that just reading the cached value isn't one of them.
images.caption: The dashed INACTIVE box shows the `gcTime` countdown.

questions.explanation: The default `gcTime` is `5 * 60 * 1000` ms, which is **5 minutes**. The timer starts only when a query becomes *inactive*, meaning its last observer (component) unmounts. If nothing subscribes again within those 5 minutes, the entry is removed and its memory is freed. If something remounts sooner, the cached data is reused, and revalidated if it's stale. This has nothing to do with `staleTime` (default `0`), which controls *freshness*, not removal. Before v5, `gcTime` was called `cacheTime`.
